newsitem.title: USA: Food Lion verdict may cool media tactics.
newsitem.headline: Food Lion verdict may cool media tactics.

text.p: A jury award of $5.5 million against ABC Television for a hidden camera report on tainted food may cool the ardor of journalists for using subterfuge in investigative reporting, media experts said Wednesday.

While the jury's decision to award punitive damages to grocer Food Lion could force journalists to be more prudent about the use of deception, it could also dampen their enthusiasm for using investigative techniques proved valuable in rooting out corporate and public corruption, experts said.

"It's not a good day for journalism. It tells us that at least the jurors in this case want to hamstring the way in which journalism operates," said Bob Steele, director of the ethics programme at The Poynter Institute for Media Studies in St. Petersburg, Fla.
The U.S. District Court jury in Greensboro, N.C., awarded Food Lion damages of $5.5 million as a result of ABC's undercover report on the supermarket chain.
The panel also awarded damages of $45,750 to be paid by two producers for the show "PrimeTime Live." ABC, a subsidiary of Walt Disney Co., said it would appeal.
Food Lion, based in Salisbury, N.C., sued ABC over a 1992 report that alleged the grocer sold spoiled meat and outdated merchandise and did not use sanitary food handling practices.

The jury last month found that ABC committed fraud, trespass and breach of loyalty when its journalists obtained jobs with Food Lion stores, one as a meat handler and the other as a delicatessen clerk. They used hidden cameras and microphones to gather information. The panel awarded about $1,400 in actual damages.

The use of deception is a legitimate and valuable tool in investigative reporting, media experts said, but only when other methods of information-gathering have been exhausted. The jury's decision could force producers to decide against the use of subterfuge in cases where it was merited.

Steele said U.S. journalism had a history of "excellent" investigative reporting in which journalists used deception to get to the truth. "It should be an exceptional case in which we are willing to lie," he said. "But in those exceptional cases ... lying may be an alternative."

Steele, who has written about the use of hidden cameras in television reporting and believes they are overused and misused in television, said the jury's decision will have an impact on all TV news organisations.
He said hidden cameras and deception should be reserved for cases of "very significant wrongdoing" which endanger public health or indicate system failure by government.
"In the best of possibilities (resulting from the Food Lion decision), producers will be less likely to use hidden cameras on stories that do not measure up," he said.

Paul McMasters, First Amendment ombudsman at the Freedom Forum, an Arlington, Va.-based media studies centre, said the result of ABC's appeal would dictate the ultimate impact of the Food Lion case on journalism.

"I certainly hope that it is overturned," he said. "While there may be some immediate visceral satisfaction in punching out the media, the real loser when the media is made less aggressive is the public."
Experts agreed the damage award also reflected a broad base of public anger toward journalism, rather than a decision on ABC's actions in the Food Lion case.
Jury foreman Greg Mack said the award was based on the falsification of job application information by the two ABC journalists.
"I'm not expecting every news station in the world to shut down and not be able to operate. But you don't have to make up information," Mack said following the judgment.
The monetary award against the two producers, coupled with a Florida jury decision in a separate case last month, was likely to send a cautionary note to TV newsmagazine producers.
"I would take that verdict to say that they (jurors) see individuals responsible as well as the organisation, that each person has a moral and legal connection," Steele said.

In the Florida case, the jury awarded damages of $10 million to BankAtlantic and its chairman, Alan Levan, who claimed he was libelled by ABC News in a broadcast about real estate investments. Part of the judgment was to be paid by the report's producer, William Willson.
